  "text": "The laundromat on Mercer Street had one machine nobody used.

Number nine. Brass buttons, cloudy glass, a coin slot sealed with solder.

When I asked the attendant about it, she handed me a strip of masking tape.

“Put your name on your basket,” she said. “Not your clothes.”

I assumed she meant theft.

At eleven, while my sheets tumbled, number nine began to fill.

Inside was the yellow coat my brother had worn the day he disappeared. He was six. I was supposed to be watching him.

I crossed the room.

The attendant caught my sleeve.

“Let it finish.”

Through the glass, the coat turned slowly. One sleeve lifted against the drum, as though someone inside it was reaching for the door.

I pulled away from her.

“You don’t understand.”

“Yes,” she said. “That’s why I work here.”

The machine stopped.

Its door clicked open, and river water spread across the tiles.

The coat lay empty on the drum’s bottom. I knew the crooked stitches where Mum had repaired its pocket.

From deep inside came my brother’s voice.

“Have you found me yet?”

I knelt in the water.

The attendant slapped masking tape across my mouth.

Something struck the drum from behind. Then again, harder.

She dragged me backward as small fingers curled around the open door.

We reached the street before I tore off the tape.

“Why couldn’t I answer?”

She locked the entrance. Her hands were shaking.

“Look at your basket.”

My name was gone from the tape.

In its place, written in my brother’s careful schoolboy letters, were the words YOU’RE IT.

Behind the glass, every machine began to empty."
